title: No peeking ahead
objectives: Build a causal mask, and test that no position can see a later one.

screens.title: Too good to be true
screens.prose: The self-attention layer of lesson 1, given token and position embeddings and a readout over the 27 symbols of makemore, is trained to predict the next symbol of names at every position. The dashed line is the bigram's dev loss, 2.4514 nats a letter. Switch between the two training runs.

state.caption: No mask: every position can see the whole window.

frames.caption: No mask: every position can see the whole window.
Causal mask: each position sees only itself and earlier ones.

screens.question: The unmasked run's training loss falls far below the bigram's. Why is that too good to be true?

options.text: Each position can read the next symbol itself, the very thing it must predict
It has memorised the training names
options.why: Memorising would show on dev data. Here even the first few hundred steps fall far below any honest model.

options.text: Attention is simply a much better model than counts
options.why: The masked run, the same model, stays near 2.35. The gap comes from what the unmasked one can see.

hints.text: Self-attention reads every position of the window, later ones too.
Position $t$'s target is token $t + 1$, which sits in the window.

feedback.correct: It peeks: the next symbol is in the window, so it copies it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What can each position see?

explain.text: Without a mask, position $t$ attends to position $t + 1$, whose token is its target, so the loss falls to about 0.16. The same weights evaluated with the mask score 6.84 on dev: useless. The masked run is honest at about 2.35.

screens.title: The causal mask
screens.prose: A **causal mask** adds $-\infty$ to the score of every key after the query before the softmax, so $e^{-\infty} = 0$ and position $t$ attends only to positions 1 to $t$. The mask for $T = 4$ is shown.
screens.question: How many query and key pairs are still allowed for $T = 4$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the cells on and below the diagonal.

byKey.all: That is every pair. The mask removes the 6 above the diagonal.
byKey.strict: That leaves out the diagonal: each position may attend to itself.

explain.text: Row $t$ keeps keys 1 to $t$, so the count is $1 + 2 + \dots + T = T(T + 1)/2$: 10 for $T = 4$. The diagonal stays: a position may read its own token.

screens.title: A longer context
screens.prose: The same rule for a context of $T = 32$ tokens, the context of a small character model.
screens.question: How many pairs are allowed?

explain.text: 528 of the 1,024 pairs survive, a little over half. A masked layer still pays for the full $T \times T$ product unless the kernel skips the masked half.

screens.title: A masked row by hand
screens.prose: Row 2 of a 4 by 4 score matrix is $(1, 2, 5, 3)$. The mask adds $(0, 0, -\infty, -\infty)$.
screens.question: What weight does query 2 put on key 1? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $1/(1 + e) = 0.2689$; key 2 gets 0.7311, and keys 3 and 4 get 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Softmax over the two allowed keys.

byKey.nomask: You took the softmax over all four. The masked keys get $e^{-\infty} = 0$.
byKey.half: The two allowed scores differ, so the weights do.

explain.text: With the mask the row is $(1, 2, -\infty, -\infty)$, and the softmax gives 0.2689, 0.7311, 0, 0. The large score 5 of key 3 does not matter: it is in the future.

screens.title: Test that nothing leaks
screens.prose: A mask is easy to get wrong, so test it: change a token after position $t$ and check that outputs 1 to $t$ do not move. In a window of 8 tokens, the token at position 6 is changed.
screens.question: Which outputs may change?

options.why: With the mask, positions 1 to 5 never see position 6.
Positions 7 and 8 attend to position 6 too, so they may change.

feedback.correct: Only positions at or after the change can see it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Who attends to position 6?

explain.text: Output $t$ depends on tokens 1 to $t$ only. A **leak test** changes a later token and asserts the earlier outputs are unchanged; a model that fails it will look brilliant in training and fail in use.

screens.title: Scored against the bigram
screens.prose: The supplied model, trained here for 3,000 steps with the mask, is scored on makemore's dev names, every next symbol once with up to 8 symbols of context: 2.2737 nats a letter. The bigram of makemore L1 scored 2.4514 on the same names.
screens.question: What is the model's dev loss in bits a letter? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the nats by $\ln 2$.

byKey.nats: That is the loss in nats. Divide by $\ln 2$.
byKey.bigram: That is the bigram in bits.
byKey.log10: You divided by $\ln 10$. Bits use base 2.

explain.text: 2.2737 nats is 3.2802 bits a letter, 0.2564 bits better than the bigram, because it reads up to 8 earlier symbols instead of one. Four heads do better still: 2.1729 nats.

screens.title: Masking after the softmax
screens.prose: A colleague applies the softmax to the full row $(1, 2, 5, 3)$ first, then zeroes the weights of keys 3 and 4.
screens.question: What do query 2's remaining weights sum to? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Add the first two weights of the full softmax.
Key 3's large score took most of the weight first.

feedback.correct: 0.0566: the row no longer sums to 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add what is left after zeroing.

byKey.one: It would be 1 if the mask came first. After the softmax, keys 3 and 4 already took their share.

explain.text: The full softmax gave keys 3 and 4 0.9434 of the weight; zeroing leaves 0.0566. Worse, the future scores already shaped the normaliser, so information leaked. Mask the scores, then take the softmax.

screens.title: The first position
screens.prose: Edge case: query 1 in a masked layer. Every key but its own is masked.
screens.question: What weight does query 1 put on itself?

hints.text: How many keys survive in row 1?
The softmax of one score is 1.

feedback.correct: 1: the first position can only read itself.

byKey.t: Equal weights over four keys ignore the mask.
byKey.zero: Its own key is on the diagonal, which the mask keeps.

explain.text: Row 1 keeps only the diagonal, so its weight is 1 and its output is its own value. That is why the first prediction of a name rests on the start mark alone.

widget.prelude:
import json
import numpy as np

with open('sequence-attn-names.json') as f:
    _W = json.load(f)
MODEL = {k: np.array(v) for k, v in _W['h1'].items()}
VOCAB = _W['vocab']


def logits_of(model, X, mask=True):
    X = np.atleast_2d(np.asarray(X))
    B, T = X.shape
    x = model['E'][X] + model['P'][:T]
    q, k, v = x @ model['Wq'], x @ model['Wk'], x @ model['Wv']
    S = q @ np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2) / np.sqrt(q.shape[-1])
    if mask:
        S = S + np.triu(np.full((T, T), -np.inf), 1)
    S = S - S.max(-1, keepdims=True)
    A = np.exp(S)
    A = A / A.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    return (A @ v) @ model['Wo'] @ model['U'] + model['c']


def model_fn(tokens):
    return logits_of(MODEL, [tokens])[0]


def leaky_fn(tokens):
    return logits_of(MODEL, [tokens], mask=False)[0]


g = np.random.default_rng(2)
Qr, Kr, Vr = g.standard_normal((5, 4)), g.standard_normal((5, 4)), g.standard_normal((5, 3))

widget.prelude:
import json
import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor
from seq_ops_l3 import attention, causal_mask

with open('sequence-attn-names.json') as f:
    _W = json.load(f)
MODEL = {k: np.array(v) for k, v in _W['h1'].items()}
SYM = _W['vocab']
IX = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(SYM)}
with open('names.txt') as f:
    _names = f.read().splitlines()
_perm = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(_names))
DEV = [_names[i] for i in _perm[25626:28829]]
TRAIN = [_names[i] for i in _perm[:25626]]


def windows(names):
    Xs, Ys = [], []
    for w in names:
        x = [0] + [IX[ch] for ch in w]
        y = [IX[ch] for ch in w] + [0]
        n = len(x)
        Xs.append(x[:8] + [0] * (8 - min(n, 8)))
        Ys.append(y[:8] + [-1] * (8 - min(n, 8)))
        for j in range(8, n):
            Xs.append(x[j - 7:j + 1])
            Ys.append([-1] * 7 + [y[j]])
    return np.array(Xs), np.array(Ys)


XDV, YDV = windows(DEV)
XTR, YTR = windows(TRAIN)


def logits_of(model, X):
    X = np.atleast_2d(np.asarray(X))
    T = X.shape[1]
    x = model['E'][X] + model['P'][:T]
    q, k, v = x @ model['Wq'], x @ model['Wk'], x @ model['Wv']
    S = q @ np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2) / np.sqrt(q.shape[-1]) + np.triu(np.full((T, T), -np.inf), 1)
    S = S - S.max(-1, keepdims=True)
    A = np.exp(S)
    A = A / A.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    return (A @ v) @ model['Wo'] @ model['U'] + model['c']


def loss_tensor(P, X, Y):
    T = X.shape[1]
    x = P['E'][X] + P['P'][np.arange(T)]
    h = attention(x @ P['Wq'], x @ P['Wk'], x @ P['Wv'], causal_mask(T)) @ P['Wo']
    z = (h @ P['U'] + P['c']).reshape(-1, 27)
    keep = (Y.reshape(-1) >= 0)
    from autograd import cross_entropy
    return cross_entropy(z[np.nonzero(keep)[0]], Y.reshape(-1)[keep])


def start_model(seed=0):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    s = 1 / np.sqrt(32)
    return {'E': g.standard_normal((27, 32)) * 0.3, 'P': g.standard_normal((8, 32)) * 0.3,
            'Wq': g.standard_normal((32, 32)) * s, 'Wk': g.standard_normal((32, 32)) * s, 'Wv': g.standard_normal((32, 32)) * s,
            'Wo': g.standard_normal((32, 32)) * s, 'U': g.standard_normal((32, 27)) * s, 'c': np.zeros(27)}


XB, YB = XTR[:256], YTR[:256]

screens.title: The look-ahead bias of a backtest
screens.prose: A researcher's daily signal uses each day's closing price to decide that same morning's trade. The backtest shows a Sharpe ratio of 4.
screens.question: What is the unmasked attention model's mistake that this backtest repeats?

options.text: Using information from after the decision: here the close, there the next token

options.why: Overfitting is a different fault; this one uses data that would not have been known.
Scaling cannot create a Sharpe ratio of 4; seeing the future can.

hints.text: A causal mask stops a position reading later tokens; a backtest needs the same rule in time.

feedback.correct: Both read the future. A forecast must use only what was known at the time (validation L2).
feedback.generic: Not quite. What did each use that it could not have known?

explain.text: The close is known only at the end of the day, so a morning trade cannot depend on it. That is look-ahead bias, the backtest's version of attending to the next token. The cure is the same: mask the future, and test that it is masked.

ideas: A causal mask adds $-\infty$ to the scores of later keys before the softmax, so position $t$ attends only to 1 to $t$: $T(T + 1)/2$ pairs, 10 for $T = 4$ and 528 for $T = 32$.

Without it a next-token model reads its own target and its training loss falls to about 0.16. With it, the supplied model scores 2.2737 nats (3.2802 bits) on the dev names against the bigram's 2.4514.
Mask before the softmax, never after; prove it with a leak test that changes later tokens and checks the earlier outputs.

formula.name: Causal attention
formula.tex: \operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{\mathbf Q\mathbf K^\top}{\sqrt d} + \mathbf M\Big)\mathbf V, \quad M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & j \le i \\ -\infty & j > i \end{cases}
formula.note: The first position reads only itself.
